source.title: Future Lens: Anticipating Subsequent Tokens from a Single Hidden State
source.authors: Koyena Pal; Jiuding Sun; Andrew Yuan; Byron C. Wallace; David Bau

record.tranche_reason: Tests future-token decodability from a single hidden state using linear readouts and hidden-state transplantation in GPT-J-6B; it is the original source for V2, not a reproduction on new models.
record.gate_note: Reports accuracy and surprisal for future-token readouts, accuracy by token category, and accuracy by model-confidence group. The cited prior-work results and the bigram baseline value are not rows because they are not results of an operation on the claim's object.
record.test_reason: This is an original source for V2. On GPT-J-6B it decodes tokens 2–4 positions ahead from one hidden state, using linear probes and hidden-state transplantation. Because it is an original source, it gets no verdict labels.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that single hidden states in GPT-J-6B encode information about tokens up to four positions ahead 'to some degree'. The learned-prompt intervention decodes this best: over 48% at N=1 against a 20.1% bigram baseline, peaking at middle layers. They offer it as the 'Future Lens' probing tool.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear prediction and causal transplantation with fixed or learned prompts on GPT-J-6B, rather than rhyme-word representation and rhyme-changing interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies by decoding method, future position N, layer, last-context-token category, and model-confidence group. Learned-prompt accuracy is reported to peak at middle layers.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning
record.problems: The study tests only GPT-J-6B, uses English data and 1000 test tokens, selects contexts where the model correctly predicts the following token, and evaluates only up to N=3. The text reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's bigram baseline result (20.1% at N=1) is not a measurement of the hidden-state representation itself. N=0 immediate next-token results are outside V2's several-positions-ahead scope.

untested.parts: Models other than GPT-J-6B. Offsets beyond four tokens. Non-English data. Contexts where the model mispredicts the next token, since the test set was selected for correct predictions.
Not tested: no rhyming verse or rhyme interventions.
Not tested: no test of whether features are computed for later positions rather than as a by-product.
Not directly tested. The study does not check whether decoded future tokens steer generation or reflect local n-gram or memorized continuations.

missing.what: Named-entity subgroup: learned-prompt accuracy is 44%, 42% and 37% for N=1, 2, 3. Authors say future information is present broadly, not only for entity names.
Learned prompt beats the best baseline by about 25 points at Precision@1, @5 and @10. Accuracy peaks at middle layers (layer 14), unlike N=0, which peaks at the last layer.
Appendix: prompts trained for N=2 or 3 perform worse at N=1, while N=1-trained prompts generalize to other N.

record.verdict_notes: This study is one of the listed original sources for V2, so it gets no supports, limits_scope or challenges labels. The reader's 'partial' states throughout are too conservative for the learned-prompt rows; set them against the 20.1% bigram baseline where one exists (N=1 only). Labelling of learned-prompt rows is inconsistent: probing in R01–R24, patching in R28 onward. Selection effects matter: the test set is only contexts the model predicts correctly, and confidence strongly moderates accuracy. Surprisal rows have no baseline, so cannot_determine is acceptable.

versions.untested_parts: Rhyming verse, candidate rhyme words, and interventions that change the line ending.
Only GPT-J-6B and English Pile samples are tested; future positions are limited to N=1, 2, 3 for the main future-token results. No broader model or task generality is tested.
Does not test whether features are computed because they help later positions rather than as a side effect of next-token prediction.
No smaller open-weight model comparison or open attribution-graph tool is tested.
No multi-step reasoning, chess, Sokoban, or other task or architecture is tested.
Does not test whether decoded information is merely local or incidental, nor whether it steers ordinary generation. It evaluates only up to N=3 in the reported future-token experiments.

rows.note: Best reported result for this method and N; accuracy values are reported as percentages in the paper's results.

relation.reason: Its own GPT-J-6B experiments measure whether individual hidden states permit decoding tokens beyond the immediate next token.

tranche.reason: Linear decoding and hidden-state transplantation test future-token information using different methods from the rhyme-representation interventions.

source_check.notes: N=0 predicts t+1; N=1–3 predict t+2–4. Intervention evaluations supply preceding generated tokens (Equations 9–11), and samples are restricted to contexts with correct next-token predictions.

statements.correction: Section 3.4: empirical Pile bigram baseline accuracy at N=1 = 20.1%; Table 2: learned-prompt, fixed-prompt, linear hidden-state and linear vocabulary comparisons.
statements.problem: The blanket statement 'no controls' overlooks the empirical bigram baseline and comparisons across decoding methods.
